title: The Punch Line
subtitle: a rag for the player piano
concept: a joke and a rag are the same machine — and for the last strain, the roll is doctored: more notes than any ten fingers.
about: A joke works by building a grid of expectation and landing just beside it. That is syncopation, described exactly. In ragtime the left hand is the setup — four beats of law, stated until the ear signs the contract — and the right hand is the comedian, accepting the grid precisely so it can land somewhere else. Stop-time is the pause before the punch line. A rag is a joke told in eighth notes.

I set it inside the machine that raised the style: the player piano. Rags were sold as punched paper, and the roll is the older sibling of the MIDI file this piece was written in — holes, positions, durations, digital music sixty years early. The roll companies kept the era's best inside joke, too: their arrangers doctored the rolls, punching in octaves and filler and fourth voices no ten fingers could reach, selling parlors a ghost with too many hands. Everyone knew. Nobody minded. The fraud became the style.

So the piece plays by two-hand rules for six strains — setup, topper, callback, an aside in sixths — then stops for one entire bar of nothing. After the pause comes the punch line, and on its repeat the ghost stops pretending: the melody doubles an octave up, tremolo thirds appear from nowhere, three registers sing at once, and a five-octave run in thirty-second notes goes by that no hand alive could play. It ends the only way it could: shave and a haircut, two bits — and one last hole punched in the roll.
Form: classic multi-strain rag in A-flat, trio in D-flat, 2/4 throughout, at Joplin's printed tempo law: it is never right to play ragtime fast.
